effect_estimate.comment: No inferential statistical model (no regression coefficients, 95% CIs, or p-values) is estimated; the paper reports descriptive municipal indicators alongside qualitative institutional comparison. Note that the cell grids of Tables 1–3 are not rendered in the PDF text layer, so exact figures are extracted strictly from the body text and footnotes.
effect_estimate.value: Descriptive comparative case findings (no inferential statistical estimate reported): Under shared management (Indaial, Law 3.218/2003 and Law 3.255/04), 99.3% of households had water supply, 1.7% had piped sewerage network connection (87.9% septic tanks), 50% of net revenues were earmarked for sanitation via a participatory Municipal Sanitation Council and Fund, low-income Social Assistance families (~1,200 eligible families) received reconnection-fee exemptions, free meter installation, and a R$2.60/month social tariff (up to 10 m³/month), non-payment disconnections were ~2%, and water production cost was R$2.1/m³. Under privatization (Itapema, 25-year concession, Edital 004/03), household public water coverage rose from 78.85% (2001) to 96% (2009) and sewerage coverage reached 59.8% (2009), but water production cost was R$2.7/m³ (28.6% higher than Indaial), no social tariff existed, meter installation cost users 7 to 25 times the Reference Water Fee (TRA), neither the Municipal Sanitation Council nor the Users' Association was implemented, and litigation/implementation disputes coincided with summer water shortages, dirty-water/sewage-leak complaints, and a proposed 38.16% tariff hike (blocked by municipal regulators).
effect_estimate.where_found: PDF Pages 7–13, Sections 'Casos comparados', 'Desenho dos dois modelos', and 'Análise e conclusões'; PDF Page 15, Note 24

mechanism_certainty.comment: Capped at ceiling 2 because the study is a qualitative comparative case study appraised with CASP. Rated 2 because primary documentary sources (CMSA monthly minutes 2004–2009, municipal statutes/bidding notices, court records, and weekly local newspaper archives 2003–2009) directly document how legal/institutional mechanisms (social tariff and reconnection exemptions, participatory council/fund earmarking, bidding litigation, meter charges, and municipal regulatory oversight) operated in practice on service coverage, affordability, continuity, and disconnections.
